newsitem.title: CANADA: Talisman CEO says Wascana bid winning kudos.
newsitem.headline: Talisman CEO says Wascana bid winning kudos.

text.p: Talisman Energy Inc. Chief Executive Jim Buckee, fresh from an eastern Canadian swing to sell investors on his C$1.7-billion ($1.3-billion) bid for Wascana Energy Inc., said on Friday both firms' shareholders were enthusiastic about the deal.

"The Wascana shareholders have said, 'Thank goodness you've come along,'" Buckee told Reuters in an interview. "Talisman shareholders have said they like it, they like the reasons, the industrial logic is good and they're well behind it."

Buckee, who has a reputation as one of the industry's shrewdest dealmakers, spent the past nine days in Toronto and Montreal running investors and analysts through the proposal that would make Talisman Canada's second-largest energy company in terms of oil and gas production.

Last week, Talisman, once the Canadian branch of British Petroleum Co. Plc, said it planned to offer C$18.50 ($13.69) cash or 0.41 of a Talisman share for each share of Regina, Saskatchewan-based Wascana.
Wascana is a former Saskatchewan government-owned company known for heavy oil production. Saskatchewan still owns 7.3 percent of the company.
Under the deal, 40 percent of Wascana shares would be bought for cash and the rest swapped for stock. Talisman would also assume about C$200 million in long-term debt.
"No shareholder in the past has ever seen anything like this," said Buckee. "Wascana was trading in the range of C$12 ($8.88)-C$13 ($9.62) for all of '95 and all of '96 until we came along."

Rumors of a Wascana takeover had circulated for several months in the Canadian oil patch before Talisman's announcement. Talisman began to plot the offer in November but had been mulling a deal for much longer.

Some Canadian and U.S. oil companies, including Alberta Energy Co. Ltd., Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd. and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd., have been rumored as potential white knights for Wascana.

But Buckee said he doubted a competitor would emerge because of a close operational fit and his firm's early groundwork in bringing on side the target's largest shareholder -- mutual fund company Altamira Management Ltd.

The offer also fits with Saskatchewan government legislation passed last year which eliminated a limit on any one shareholder owning more than 10 percent of Wascana's stock. One stipulation that remained, however, was that Wascana's headquarters must remain in Regina.
Talisman plans to make Wascana a wholly owned subsidiary, add headquarters staff and set up a heavy oil research program at the University of Regina.

The deal's size -- it would be the largest takeover in the Canadian energy industry since Talisman absorbed Bow Valley Energy for C$1.8 billion ($1.3 billion) in 1994 -- would also limit the list of other potential suitors, Buckee said.
Talisman plans to mail its takeover documents to shareholders late next week and a Wascana official said his firm would not comment until its board had looked over the offer.
Buckee anticipated Wascana's directors would eventually recommend the deal. "Their fiduciary duty is to do the best by their shareholders and this is it," he said.
Wascana shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange were trading on Friday up C10 cents (7 cents) to C$18.70 ($13.84). Talisman was up C85 cents (63 cents) to C$45 ($33.30).
